openers.roots-and-the-rhizosphere: Half of a plant lives in the dark. Its roots anchor it, take in water and dissolved nutrients, and spread through the soil as one thick central root or a dense mat of thin ones, steered by gravity, light, barriers and soil conditions. Fine outgrowths of single cells do much of the collecting, and roots can even move water from moist soil into dry. Roots also release sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA into the soil around them. This chapter follows those compounds into the narrow zone they shape, crowded with microbes, and into the legume family, about 19,000 species including soybean, pea and alfalfa.

soil-bio-133.title: Roots, the hidden half that anchors and feeds a plant
soil-bio-133.text: Roots left their mark in rock long before any animal walked on land. Fossil roots go back to the late Silurian, about 430 million years ago. Most are voids that filled in after the roots rotted, and they are easily confused with animal burrows. A root is the plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients. Its skin cells, the epidermis, and their fine outgrowths, described in {{ref:soil-bio-140}}, take up soil water and dissolved ions. These then travel to the shoot through the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. Roots also store reserves and make growth regulators. A cap of cells guards each growing tip and helps the new root push through soil. As the root deepens, the cap sheds cells and leaves a slimy, lubricating surface. The depth and spread of a root system decide which soil horizons the plant can draw water and nutrients from. Roots rarely work alone. Most vascular plants partner with certain fungi, described in {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and bacteria and many other organisms live close to roots too. On rangeland, grass roots hold soil together and reduce erosion. When the old roots of perennial grasses decay, they add organic matter and release nutrients.

soil-bio-182.title: The legume family and its nitrogen-making guests
soil-bio-182.text: About 19,000 species of flowering plants share one underground talent. The legume or pea family, Fabaceae, includes soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa. Many legumes host bacteria, described in {{ref:soil-bio-178}}, in small swellings on their roots. These guests take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use. The swellings are common across the family, though rarer in the Caesalpinioideae, and some species in every subfamily lack them. One plant can host several kinds: those of Acacia senegal can hold seven bacterial species from three genera. That talent is why farmers rotate crops with legumes and why green-manure crops are commonly legumes.

soil-bio-139.title: Taproots, the single deep anchor
soil-bio-139.text: Snap a dandelion off at ground level and it simply grows back. Its taproot survives below: a large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, with smaller roots branching sideways. Unless that root is cut several centimeters down, the weed resprouts. Dicots, plants with two seed leaves, start life with a taproot grown from the seed's first root, the radicle. It may last the plant's life but is more often replaced by {{ref:soil-bio-138}}. Soil shapes it. Deep, rich soils favor vertical taproots in many oaks, while clay soils promote several. Carrot, radish and turnip are taproots built for storage.

soil-bio-138.title: Fibrous roots, the dense mat near the surface
soil-bio-138.text: A mature tree 30–50 m tall spreads its roots as far as its height or more, yet well over 95% of them lie in the top 50 cm. Within a few years, most trees switch from a taproot to this wide, shallow kind of network. A fibrous root system is a dense mat of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base, the opposite of a taproot system. It forms when the embryonic root dies back while the plant is young, leaving fine roots and no distinct taproot. In many species most of the mat is adventitious roots, roots that sprout from the stem base. Monocots, the flowering plants with one seed leaf, all have one, as do ferns; wheat and rice are typical. Fibrous roots bind soil, take up surface nutrients quickly and control erosion. Forage crops cover a whole field and anchor its top layer of soil. The root mats of meadow grasses may even help hold radioactive materials in place.

soil-bio-136.title: How roots feel their way through the soil
soil-bio-136.text: Roots are not blind diggers. They sense gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and they steer their growth in response. Gravitropism, growth guided by gravity and worked through the plant hormone auxin, sends roots downward from germination. Each root type holds its own set angle. Air, nutrients and water pull roots toward them, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil. Roots hunting for nutrients can sense compacted soil through the diffusion of ethylene gas, and avoid it. They can even tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil. Given years, roots crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

soil-bio-134.title: Root system architecture, the shape of the hidden half
soil-bio-134.text: Two plants in one field can lay out their roots in entirely different shapes. Root system architecture is that layout: how a plant's whole root system branches, spreads and angles through the soil. It is described by branching pattern (herringbone, dichotomous or radial) and by link length between branches, link radius and root angle. The species, the soil's composition and the nutrients on offer all shape it. So do gravity, light, water and oxygen, and the supply or lack of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, aluminum and sodium chloride. A system built in dry soil may work less well when the soil floods.

soil-bio-135.title: How deep roots go, and what stops them
soil-bio-135.text: The deepest living root ever observed turned up in an open-pit mine in Arizona, at least 60 meters (200 ft) down. Rooting depth describes how a plant's roots spread down through the soil. It depends on the plant's form, on where and when water and nutrients are available, and on the {{ref:soil-phys-040}}. Most roots of most plants still lie fairly close to the surface, where nutrients are more available and aeration is better. Rock, compacted soil just below the surface or a lack of oxygen can physically stop them. Deserts and temperate coniferous forests generally have the deepest roots; tundra, boreal forest and temperate grasslands the shallowest. In continuous permafrost, roots cannot pass below the thin top layer that thaws each summer. Plants there must be shallow-rooted, and trees are limited to specialists such as larch. Some roots grow as deep as their tree is tall.

soil-bio-137.title: Roots that breathe, pull, prop and store
soil-bio-137.text: Not every root just anchors and drinks. Specialized roots take on other tasks; they include aerial, prop, buttress, storage and contractile roots, and the tufts described in {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. Those tufts of short rootlets form when phosphate or iron runs low, notably in the Proteaceae. Mangroves raise aerating roots, or pneumatophores, above ground or water to exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited. Contractile roots expand sideways and shorten lengthwise, pulling bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper. Swellings in virtually all legumes, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Coralloid roots near the surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

soil-bio-140.title: Root hairs, where most of the water comes in
soil-bio-140.text: Most of the water a root takes in passes through hairs finer than a pencil line. A root hair is a thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell near the root tip. Each is 15–17 micrometers across and 80–1,500 micrometers long, long enough to reach in between soil particles. Together they raise the root's surface area relative to its volume. They grow only in the zone of maturation, perhaps because older hairs are sheared off as the root pushes on. Root hair cells secrete malic and citric acids, which change the oxidation state of minerals so their ions are easier to absorb. The hairs are also the main meeting point with fungal partners, described in {{ref:soil-bio-157}}. In legumes they curl around bacteria so that an infection thread can grow inward and start a nodule. Transplanting or repotting can strip many hairs off and make the plant wilt.

soil-bio-187.title: Roots that move water from wet soil to dry
soil-bio-187.text: During a drought, a deep-rooted plant can draw up groundwater and release it into parched topsoil. Hydraulic redistribution is this passive movement of water by roots from moist soil to dry soil. It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil. It is strongest in those with taproots reaching the water table and lateral roots near the surface. In drought, water rises up the taproot and seeps from the laterals into the dry surface soil. Under flooding, roots move water the other way. The xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, links taproot to laterals. Wet or dry soil around the laterals then sets up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull, the tug of water evaporating from leaves. It was once described as hydraulic lift: roots releasing water and nutrients into soil, mostly at night. Researchers now see two-way movement, helped by fungal networks described in {{ref:soil-bio-164}}. Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis, an inner sheath of root cells, and by stomata, the pores in leaves. Cavitation, air breaking the water column in the xylem, can stop it. By smoothing out differences in soil moisture, the process affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish. Scientists trace it with deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, and with sap flow and soil moisture measurements. Efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

soil-bio-142.title: Root exudates, the food roots give away
soil-bio-142.text: Roots leak food into the soil on purpose. Root exudates are the organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that roots release into the surrounding soil. They help protect roots against bacterial and fungal infection and help them push through the soil. They can also create a microclimate that benefits the plant. Exudates feed microbial activity and add carbon to the soil. Organic acids among them change the chemistry and the living communities right next to the root, compared with soil farther away. Each plant species releases its own mix and so recruits its own microbes from the surrounding soil. Root and microbial exudates can even extract phosphorus from apatite, the most common mineral source of soil phosphorus. One group, described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}}, works with soil phosphorus to steer how fungal threads grow through the soil.

soil-bio-143.title: The rhizosphere, the crowded zone around every root
soil-bio-143.text: Each gram of soil in and around roots can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that grow in culture. In 1904 the German plant physiologist Lorenz Hiltner named this crowded zone the rhizosphere. He meant soil around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release. Today it is defined as the narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms living with the roots. The roots pay generously for their company. They may exude 20–40% of the carbon they fix by photosynthesis as sugars and organic acids. Microbes in the zone's pores feed on these root exudates and on sloughed-off root cells, a process described in {{ref:soil-bio-148}}. The result is a hotspot of microbial diversity. Much of the nutrient cycling plants need happens right beside roots, and so does disease suppression by microbial antibiotics. Organic acids and sugars affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available. Root respiration and exudation can create pockets without oxygen next to roots. In acid soils, the pH rises close to roots. At the very center lies the rhizoplane: the root surface itself, with the soil particles closely bound to it.

soil-bio-157.title: Mycorrhiza, the ancient pact between root and fungus
soil-bio-157.text: In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus reaches the plant through fungi. A mycorrhiza is the partnership behind those numbers. It is a symbiosis in which fungal hyphae, the fungus's fine threads, interconnect with plant roots and meet them at the level of single cells. The plant pays the fungus in sugars or lipids made by photosynthesis, perhaps 20–40% of its carbon. The fungus returns water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc. Some fungi colonize root tissue inside the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Others grow between the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. The partnership occurs in 92% of plant families studied, covering 80% of species. Some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form it at all. A plant short of phosphorus is quick to recruit fungi, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part. The deal is normally mutualistic, good for both sides, but in some species or circumstances it turns parasitic. It is also ancient. Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and early fungal partners may have been key to plants colonizing land.

soil-bio-149.title: Bulk soil, the quiet ground beyond the roots
soil-bio-149.text: Step away from a root and the soil goes quiet. Bulk soil is the soil outside the rhizosphere, not penetrated by plant roots. Natural organic compounds are much scarcer there. Its microbes are more varied but less abundant than those near roots, and bulk-soil organisms are generally smaller than the same species beside roots. Most bacteria here are quiescent. They rest in slimy colonies glued together with clay particles, which protect them from drying out and from grazing protozoa and nematodes. Bulk soil tends to have smaller pores and to hold more moisture at a given matric potential than the rhizosphere, which affects which microbes survive. Its chemistry is described by organic matter, organic carbon, nutrient content, cation-exchange capacity, free ions, pH and base saturation. Its respiration responds to temperature swings. Added nutrients or warming can strongly change its microbes, especially in sandy soils.

soil-bio-158.title: Sugar for minerals: how the mycorrhizal trade works
soil-bio-158.text: Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair. That fineness is the fungus's whole advantage. Mycorrhizal nutrient exchange is the trade in which the fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals. Sugars such as glucose and sucrose travel from their source, usually the leaves, down to the roots and on to the fungus. In exchange, the hyphae explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface. They may secrete organic acids that dissolve or chelate ions, or free ions from minerals by ion exchange. They reach phosphate and iron that roots alone cannot, including nutrients immobilized in clay-rich or strongly basic soils. Some mycorrhizal fungi decay organic matter directly. In some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing the soil. Farmers can lean on the trade. Inga alley cropping, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on the fungi in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil. The trade helps most in nutrient-poor soils. Yet in boreal forests the fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the deal may be more than simply mutualistic.

soil-bio-161.title: Fungal partners as bodyguards against stress
soil-bio-161.text: A fungal partner is also a bodyguard. Mycorrhizal fungi protect plants against soil-borne disease, drought, salt and toxic metals. Mycorrhizal plants often resist soil-borne pathogens better, and the fungi secrete enzymes toxic to soil organisms such as nematodes. Forming the partnership primes the plant's immune system, so its defense responses are stronger. In one study the fungi tracked soil water level rather than aggregate stability, and they can make plants more resistant to drought. Salt can harm the fungi, yet many reports show mycorrhizal plants growing better under salt stress. The fungi also shield plants rooted in acidic, contaminated or metal-rich soils. Pines inoculated with Pisolithus tinctorius tolerated contaminated sites well. Zinc-tolerant Suillus bovinus protected Scots pine, probably by binding the metal in its external mycelium without blocking useful exchange.

soil-bio-159.title: Inside the cell or around it: the kinds of mycorrhiza
soil-bio-159.text: The first question about any mycorrhiza is how far the fungus gets into the root. Mycorrhizal types group these partnerships by how the fungus colonizes the root. The main split runs between {{ref:soil-bio-173}} and endomycorrhizas. In the first kind, the hyphae never enter individual root cells. In endomycorrhizas they pass through the cell wall, up to the cell membrane. The endomycorrhizas include the types described in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}, {{ref:soil-bio-176}} and {{ref:soil-bio-186}}, along with arbutoid and monotropoid forms. The lifestyle evolved independently many times. The fungi of the first of those endomycorrhizal types form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life. Not every fungus inside a root is a partner of this kind. Fungal endophytes live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside. Mucoromycotina 'fine root endophytes' were long mistaken for partners of the first type. They seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils. In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the flow runs backward. The plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

soil-bio-166.title: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, the most widespread plant partnership
soil-bio-166.text: Earth's topsoils hold an estimated 110 quadrillion kilometers of one kind of fungal thread. It belongs to the arbuscular mycorrhiza, the most widespread plant symbiosis known. In this type the fungus enters the cortical cells of a root, the cells of its outer tissue layer, and builds tree-like arbuscules inside them. Arbuscules are where nutrients and carbon change hands; balloon-like vesicles often store reserves. The fungi, from the Glomeromycotina and some Mucoromycotina, help plants capture phosphorus, sulfur, nitrogen and micronutrients. They partner 80% of vascular plant families and about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica. The fungi are obligate symbionts with little ability to live on dead matter, and up to 20% of the host's carbon may pass to them. About 40% of their hyphae lie in wild grasslands, and the total holds about 300 megatons of carbon. They are vital on poor volcanic soils and sand dunes. Their hyphae and a soil protein described in {{ref:soil-bio-121}} improve soil aggregate stability.

soil-bio-173.title: Ectomycorrhiza, the fungal sheath of forest trees
soil-bio-173.text: Only about 2% of plant species form ectomycorrhizas, yet they include trees that dominate whole ecosystems. In this kind of mycorrhiza the fungus sheathes the root tip and grows between the root's outer cells without entering them. The fungi, mostly Basidiomycota and Ascomycota, build a mantle up to 40 μm thick and a net between epidermal and cortical cells, described in {{ref:soil-bio-185}}. Their hyphae reach several centimeters into the soil. Hosts are mostly woody plants such as birch, beech, willow and pine. Nitrogen is scarce in most ecosystems and locked in hard-to-break-down organic matter. The fungi reach further than roots and extract it from the organic layer. They receive an estimated 15% of the host's food and supply up to 86% of its nitrogen needs. Heavy fertilizer nitrogen breaks the deal: in one study, fungal species fell from over 30 at low-nitrogen sites to 9 at high-nitrogen sites. Laccaria bicolor even lures and kills springtails; eastern white pine inoculated with it got up to 25% of its nitrogen from them.

soil-bio-177.title: Glomeromycota, the fungi behind most root partnerships
soil-bio-177.text: About 230 described species of fungi partner the roots of most of the world's plants. They make up the Glomeromycota, the group whose members form arbuscular mycorrhizas. They live in soils worldwide, partnering over 80% of plant species, even in salt marshes. Most evidence shows they depend on land plants for carbon and energy, which long made them hard to grow in the laboratory. They reproduce asexually by spores 80–500 μm across, and new colonization tracks the density of spores in the soil. A survey of arid land found 5.4% of fungal rRNA reads were Glomeromycota, suggesting earlier PCR-based studies had underestimated them.
